title: Systems of Equations
coreInsight: Several unknown quantities can be determined when several independent constraints must hold simultaneously.
targetLearnerRealization: One equation can allow many pairs, while a second independent equation can select the unique pair that makes both relationships true.
learningObjectives: Explain why one equation with two unknown quantities may have several solutions.
Represent two independent constraints as a system of equations.
Eliminate a variable by adding or subtracting equal relationships.
Use substitution as an alternative way to preserve the system's shared solution.
Check a candidate pair in every original equation and story condition.

continuity.openingCallback: Continue the shelf question by making several pairs satisfy one total before a new fact narrows them.
closingSeeds: A solution to a system belongs to every constraint at once.
Combining equations can remove a quantity while preserving the shared solution.
More unknown quantities generally require more independent information.

misconceptionTargets.misconception: One equation usually determines two unknown quantities.
A variable can take a different value in each equation of the same system.
Elimination is symbol manipulation unrelated to preserving the same solution set.
Finding one plausible pair is enough without checking every constraint.

beats.purpose: Make the underdetermination of one equation visible before naming systems.
beats.expectedRealization: A total of seven riders permits eight bicycle/tricycle splits.
beats.transitionIn: The equation n + b = 18 allowed many book pairs. Try the same idea with seven riders choosing between two kinds of vehicle.
beats.prompt: Seven children each ride either a bicycle or a tricycle. If b is the number of bicycles and t is the number of tricycles, how many nonnegative whole-number pairs (b, t) satisfy b + t = 7?
beats.correctFeedback: Yes. The tricycle count can be any whole number from 0 through 7, with the bicycle count filling the rest.
beats.incorrectFeedback: List the possible tricycle counts from none to all seven and pair each with the remaining bicycles.

visual.ariaLabel: Eight paired bicycle and tricycle counts that total seven riders

steps.title: Cover every split
steps.body: t can be 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, or 7. For each choice, b = 7 - t. These eight cases cover every allowed tricycle count and no pair repeats.

resolution.takeaway: One total equation can describe several pairs of unknown quantities.

beats.purpose: Use the approved vehicle problem to let a second independent count select one split.
beats.expectedRealization: The wheel total rules out seven of the eight rider splits.
beats.whyNow: Seven riders alone has just produced eight candidates; the authentic wheel count supplies the missing independent constraint.
beats.entryBridge: The rider count leaves eight possibilities. Now require the same pair to account for nineteen wheels.
beats.exitBridge: Five tricycles and two bicycles satisfy both counts; now translate the two filters into equations.
beats.reusedRepresentation: Seven vehicle slots whose bicycle/tricycle split changes while the rider total remains fixed.
learnerPrompts: What wheel total results if all seven riders begin on bicycles?
How many wheels short of nineteen is that arrangement?
Why does each bicycle-to-tricycle swap add exactly one wheel?
After five swaps, how many bicycles remain?
How does the split satisfy both the rider and wheel totals?
Which answer follows from the verified split?
beats.correctFeedback: Correct. Five tricycles and two bicycles give seven riders and nineteen wheels.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Keep all seven riders fixed. Replacing one bicycle with one tricycle adds exactly one wheel.

steps.title: Write both constraints
steps.body: Let b count bicycles and t count tricycles. The riders give b + t = 7. The wheels give 2b + 3t = 19.

steps.title: Prepare to eliminate
steps.body: Double the entire rider equation: 2b + 2t = 14. It has the same solution pairs as b + t = 7.

steps.title: Subtract equal relationships
steps.body: Subtract 2b + 2t = 14 from 2b + 3t = 19. The b terms cancel and t = 5.

steps.title: Check the pair
steps.body: Then b = 2. The pair satisfies 2 + 5 = 7 and 2(2) + 3(5) = 19.

steps.title: Another way
steps.body: Start with seven bicycles and fourteen wheels. Every swap to a tricycle adds one wheel, so the five-wheel gap requires five tricycles.

resolution.takeaway: The solution is the pair that survives both independent constraints.

beats.purpose: Distinguish a pair that satisfies one constraint from the shared solution.
beats.expectedRealization: A system solution must satisfy both equations simultaneously.
beats.transitionIn: The pair (5, 2) can fit one equation depending on which number names which vehicle. Keep the variable meanings fixed and test both claims.
beats.prompt: Here b means bicycles and t means tricycles. Which pair satisfies both b + t = 7 and 2b + 3t = 19?
beats.correctFeedback: Right. Only (2, 5) gives both seven vehicles and nineteen wheels.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Substitute each ordered pair into both equations, keeping b first and t second.

steps.title: Test (5, 2)
steps.body: It passes 5 + 2 = 7 but gives 2(5) + 3(2) = 16 wheels, so it fails the second constraint.

steps.title: Test (2, 5)
steps.body: It gives 2 + 5 = 7 and 2(2) + 3(5) = 19, so it satisfies both.

resolution.takeaway: Passing one equation is not enough; the same ordered pair must pass every equation.

beats.purpose: Connect elimination to a justified equivalent-equation operation.
beats.expectedRealization: Multiplying an entire equation preserves its solutions and can align coefficients.
beats.prompt: To eliminate b from b + t = 7 and 2b + 3t = 19, which equivalent form of the first equation aligns the b terms?
beats.correctFeedback: Yes. Every term on both sides is doubled, so the same pairs remain solutions.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Multiplying an equation by two must double every term on both complete sides.

steps.title: Scale the complete equality
steps.body: Two copies of b + t = 7 give 2b + 2t = 14. Any pair satisfying one satisfies the other.

resolution.takeaway: Align coefficients by applying a valid operation to an entire equation.

beats.purpose: Make elimination arise from subtracting two true equalities side by side.
beats.expectedRealization: Subtracting corresponding sides cancels one variable and preserves the common solution.
beats.correctFeedback: Correct. The matching 2b contributions cancel, leaving one t equal to 5.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Subtract corresponding left sides and corresponding right sides: (2b + 3t) - (2b + 2t) and 19 - 14.

steps.title: Subtract corresponding totals
steps.body: Because both equations are true for the shared pair, their difference is also true: (2b + 3t) - (2b + 2t) = 19 - 14.

steps.title: See what remains
steps.body: The 2b terms and two of the three t terms cancel, leaving t = 5.

resolution.takeaway: Elimination removes equal contributions from two constraints; it does not discard information arbitrarily.

beats.purpose: Name systems and elimination after the shared-solution structure is visible.
beats.expectedRealization: A system collects constraints whose common solutions matter, and elimination preserves that intersection.
beats.name: System of equations and elimination
beats.conciseDefinition: A system of equations asks for values that make all its equations true at the same time. Elimination combines equivalent relationships so one variable cancels.
beats.formalization: b + t = 7 and 2b + 3t = 19 share the solution (b, t) = (2, 5).
beats.memoryHook: Same meanings, same pair, every constraint.

beats.purpose: Show substitution as a second shared-solution-preserving method.
beats.expectedRealization: Replacing a variable by an equal expression preserves both constraints in one equation.
beats.transitionIn: Elimination aligned equal contributions. The rider equation also offers a direct expression for either vehicle count.
beats.prompt: From b + t = 7, we know b = 7 - t. Which substitution correctly places that same bicycle count into 2b + 3t = 19?
beats.correctFeedback: Exactly. Since b and 7 - t are equal, replacing b by 7 - t keeps the wheel equation true for the same pair.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Replace the complete occurrence of b in the wheel equation with the expression equal to b.

steps.title: Substitute an equal expression
steps.body: 2(7 - t) + 3t = 19 simplifies to 14 - 2t + 3t = 19, so t = 5.

steps.title: Recover the other value
steps.body: Then b = 7 - 5 = 2. This is the same shared pair found by elimination.

resolution.takeaway: Substitution replaces a quantity with an equal expression while keeping one shared solution.

beats.purpose: Directly repair the idea that a variable may change meaning or value between equations.
beats.expectedRealization: Each variable has one meaning and one candidate value throughout a system.
beats.prompt: A learner says, “In b + t = 7, let b = 3, but in 2b + 3t = 19, let b = 2.” What is the problem?

options.text: There is no problem because equations are separate lines.
b must name the bicycle count consistently, so one candidate pair must be tested in both equations.
Variables cannot appear in more than one equation.

beats.correctFeedback: Right. The equations describe the same group of riders, so b cannot switch values between them.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Ask whether both equations describe the same bicycles and tricycles or two unrelated situations.

steps.title: Keep quantities attached to the story
steps.body: b is one bicycle count and t is one tricycle count. A system solution is a single ordered pair used everywhere.

resolution.takeaway: Variables keep the same meaning and value across every equation in a system.

beats.expectedRealization: A complete check verifies every equation and the variable meanings.
beats.prompt: Which check is sufficient to prove that (b, t) = (2, 5) solves the rider system?

options.text: 2 + 5 = 7 and 2(2) + 3(5) = 19, with b and t interpreted correctly
The answer appears among the choices

beats.correctFeedback: Yes. Every original constraint and both variable meanings are verified.
beats.incorrectFeedback: A system has more than one condition; a complete check must return to all of them.

steps.title: Verify both filters
steps.body: Two bicycles and five tricycles give seven riders. Their wheels total 4 + 15 = 19. Both variables retain their stated meanings.

resolution.takeaway: A plausible pair becomes a solution only after it passes every original constraint.

beats.purpose: Transfer combining constraints to a disguised system where the desired total appears twice.
beats.expectedRealization: Adding all three pair equations counts each unknown exactly twice.
beats.transitionIn: The vehicle equations were combined to cancel a quantity. These three weight equations can be combined to expose a quantity instead.
beats.whyNow: The approved transfer rewards reading how often each unknown appears across the complete set of constraints rather than mechanically isolating every box.
beats.entryBridge: Name the box weights a, b, and c. The scale gives a + b = 122, b + c = 125, and a + c = 127.
beats.exitBridge: The combined equation found the requested total without first finding each individual box weight.
beats.reusedRepresentation: Several equations with fixed variable meanings, combined while preserving their shared solution.
learnerPrompts: Which three boxes and three pairings are present?
How does each edge record one pair weight?
What is the sum of all three pair weights?
Why does each box appear in exactly two of the added equations?
How does halving recover the weight of all three boxes once?
beats.correctFeedback: Correct. The three pair weights total 374 pounds, which counts every box twice, so the boxes total 187 pounds.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Add the three pair equations and count how many times each individual box weight appears.

steps.title: Add all three constraints
steps.body: Adding a + b = 122, b + c = 125, and a + c = 127 gives 2a + 2b + 2c = 374.

steps.title: Interpret before dividing
steps.body: The left side is 2(a + b + c): each box appears in two pairings. Therefore a + b + c = 374 ÷ 2 = 187 pounds.

steps.title: Independent check
steps.body: The individual weights are 62, 60, and 65 pounds, whose pair sums are 122, 125, and 127 and whose total is 187.

resolution.takeaway: Combining every constraint can expose the desired quantity even when the individual unknowns are unnecessary.

beats.purpose: Assess a near heads-and-legs system with a complete check.
beats.whyNow: Return to two kinds of object with a fixed count and a weighted count.
beats.entryBridge: Replace vehicles and wheels with animals and legs while keeping the two-constraint structure.
beats.exitBridge: The pair must account for both twelve animals and thirty-four legs.
learnerPrompts: Which pair satisfies both the animal count and the leg count?
beats.correctFeedback: Correct. Five rabbits and seven chickens give twelve animals and thirty-four legs.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Start with twelve two-legged chickens, then count how many two-leg upgrades are needed to reach thirty-four legs.

steps.title: Write the system
steps.body: If c and r count chickens and rabbits, then c + r = 12 and 2c + 4r = 34.

steps.title: Eliminate and check
steps.body: Double the first equation and subtract: 2r = 10, so r = 5 and c = 7. Then 7 + 5 = 12 and 2(7) + 4(5) = 34.

resolution.takeaway: Use both constraints to determine and verify the pair.

beats.purpose: Assess a near item-count and value-count system with consistent units.
beats.whyNow: Vary the weighted count and require the same pair in cents and coins.
beats.entryBridge: The second constraint now measures value rather than legs or wheels.
beats.exitBridge: A cents check and a coin-count check confirm the same pair.
learnerPrompts: How can you write both equations using cents throughout?
beats.correctFeedback: Correct. Seven quarters and seven dimes make fourteen coins worth 245 cents.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Use d + q = 14 and 10d + 25q = 245 with the same d and q in both equations.

steps.title: Write and eliminate
steps.body: d + q = 14 and 10d + 25q = 245. Multiply the first equation by 10 and subtract it from the value equation: 15q = 105, so q = 7.

steps.title: Check
steps.body: Then d = 7. There are 7 + 7 = 14 coins worth 7(10) + 7(25) = 245 cents.

resolution.takeaway: Keep variable meanings and units fixed across both equations.

beats.purpose: Assess elimination by scaling an entire equation before subtraction.
beats.whyNow: Increase the coefficient gap so the learner must justify how equations are aligned.
beats.entryBridge: Ticket counts and ticket revenue provide two independent totals.
beats.exitBridge: Both the number sold and the money collected verify the result.
learnerPrompts: Which multiple of the ticket-count equation will align one coefficient with the revenue equation?
beats.correctFeedback: Correct. Nine adult tickets and eleven child tickets produce twenty tickets and 127 dollars.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Let a + c = 20 and 8a + 5c = 127. Scale the complete first equation before subtracting.

steps.title: Align and eliminate
steps.body: Multiply a + c = 20 by 5 to get 5a + 5c = 100. Subtract from 8a + 5c = 127, giving 3a = 27 and a = 9.

steps.title: Recover and check
steps.body: Then c = 11. The counts give 9 + 11 = 20 and the revenue gives 8(9) + 5(11) = 127.

resolution.takeaway: Scale every term in an equation, then subtract corresponding sides.

beats.purpose: Assess direct equation addition as an elimination strategy.
beats.whyNow: Use opposite coefficients that cancel without preliminary scaling.
beats.entryBridge: These constraints describe a sum and a difference rather than object counts.
beats.exitBridge: The ordered pair passes both the sum and difference checks.
learnerPrompts: What cancels when the two equations are added corresponding side to corresponding side?
beats.correctFeedback: Correct. Adding the equations gives 2x = 30, so x = 15 and y = 8.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Add x + y = 23 and x - y = 7; the y terms are opposites.

steps.title: Add the constraints
steps.body: Adding x + y = 23 and x - y = 7 gives 2x = 30, so x = 15.

resolution.takeaway: Opposite contributions disappear when corresponding sides are added.

beats.purpose: Assess challenge modeling, system solution, and a derived geometric quantity.
beats.whyNow: Finish with constraints whose solution must be used to answer a new question.
beats.entryBridge: Now the unknown pair describes side lengths, and the requested value is their product.
beats.exitBridge: The dimensions must satisfy both geometry constraints before their area is trusted.
learnerPrompts: How does perimeter 34 become a sum equation for length and width?
beats.correctFeedback: Correct. The dimensions are 11 by 6, so the area is 66 square units.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Use l + w = 17 from the perimeter and l - w = 5 from the side difference, then find the area.

steps.title: Translate both constraints
steps.body: Perimeter 34 gives 2l + 2w = 34, or l + w = 17. The length condition gives l - w = 5.

steps.title: Add and solve
steps.body: Adding the equations gives 2l = 22, so l = 11. Then w = 6.

steps.title: Check before answering
steps.body: The perimeter is 2(11) + 2(6) = 34 and the difference is 11 - 6 = 5. The area is 11 × 6 = 66.

resolution.takeaway: Solve and check the shared pair before using it to compute a requested quantity.

beats.purpose: Consolidate the meaning and proof obligations of system solving.
beats.expectedRealization: A reliable system solution represents, combines, recovers, and checks without changing variable meanings.
beats.transitionIn: Vehicles, boxes, animals, coins, tickets, numbers, and rectangles all required one pair to survive several filters. Gather the safeguards.
beats.prompt: Which actions belong in a reliable system-solving plan? Select all four.

options.text: Keep each variable's meaning fixed across every equation.
Translate each independent condition into its own relationship.
Use substitution or elimination in ways that preserve the shared solution.
Test the same ordered pair in every original condition.

response.feedback: Each action guards one part of the shared-solution argument.

beats.correctFeedback: Yes—fix meanings, represent every constraint, preserve the intersection, and check the same pair everywhere.
beats.incorrectFeedback: All four are needed to show that the final pair belongs to every original constraint.

visual.ariaLabel: Four safeguards for solving a system of equations

steps.title: Why the check matters
steps.body: An algebraic step can be correct while an original condition was translated incorrectly. Substitution into every starting relationship catches both kinds of error.

resolution.takeaway: A system solution is one pair that satisfies every constraint at the same time.

beats.purpose: Generalize the lesson's central tension without inventing an unapproved curricular successor.
beats.expectedRealization: A new unknown usually creates freedom that another independent constraint must remove.
beats.transitionIn: Two independent constraints often pinned down two unknown quantities. Add one more unknown and ask what information is missing.
beats.prompt: Suppose bicycles, tricycles, and four-wheeled carts carry 12 riders altogether, while their vehicles have 31 wheels altogether. Why might those two totals still allow several different triples?
beats.takeaway: Each independent constraint removes some freedom; extra unknown quantities generally need extra independent information.

notes: Design: A2's two-unknown shelf question leads to seven riders with eight possible splits. The nineteen-wheel constraint creates the realization that a system solution lies in every constraint. With no named curriculum successor, the closing generalizes to three unknowns rather than promising a specific next lesson.

Beat outline: enumerate rider splits -> authentic vehicle anchor -> test ordered pairs -> scale an equation -> subtract constraints -> name systems/elimination -> substitution connection -> fixed-variable-meaning check -> full-system check -> authentic box transfer -> five independent problems -> consolidation -> three-unknown reflection.
The vehicle animation and box animation appear only after answer submission. Their six and five learner prompts respectively match every declared scene state, preventing pre-response answer leakage.
The primary vehicle solution uses elimination; the all-bicycle swap animation follows as an elegant alternative connected to the learner's concrete counting knowledge.

Existing generic choice-grid visuals and response primitives suffice; no renderer or schema changes were required. Generated answers were verified by equation solving and independently by direct enumeration, substitution, or geometric reconstruction.
